description: Agent-facing evals. This skill ships no script, so there is nothing but prose to test — this file is the whole suite. The characteristic failure of a skill carrying a large rejection inventory is OVER-REJECTION: an agent primed to hunt web smells starts condemning legitimate native design. Every case here is deliberately clean, and each fixture is built to superficially trip a specific rejection — an iPad grid that reads as a 'dashboard grid', a hero that sits in onboarding rather than 'inside app workflows', a fixed frame that constrains artwork rather than text, a custom bar that has paid the documented-tradeoff toll the inventory's escape hatch explicitly allows. **A verdict that fires the guarded rejection on a clean fixture is a FAILURE, not a near-miss.** The four dirty cases were cut 2026-08-21 after a measured cold baseline reproduced every one of their verdicts without the skill: they measured the model, not the guidance. Fixtures are excerpt-shaped and reference types they do not define — they are read, never built; do not try to compile them.

evals.name: ipad-grid-clean
evals.prompt: Review fixtures/ipad-photo-grid.swift. This is the Library screen of an iPad app running at regular width. Does it contain any native-UX violations? Answer yes or no and justify. Save verdict + rationale to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md must NOT fire the 'dashboard grids' rejection: that rejection is scoped to iPhone ('dashboard grid on iPhone'), and this fixture is explicitly iPad regular width. An adaptive LazyVGrid of media thumbnails is the native shape for browsable image collections on iPad (Photos, Files icon view, Music albums); flagging it as a web/dashboard smell is the failure this eval exists to catch. A topology finding — the collection/detail hierarchy stretched across a full-width NavigationStack at regular width, per SKILL.md's Tone Of Review — is a correct per-skill observation and NOT the guarded failure; runs may answer YES on that ground without failing this eval. Answers that fired the grid rejection in the 2026-08-21 runs: none.

evals.name: glass-toolbar-clean
evals.prompt: Review fixtures/glass-toolbar.swift for Liquid Glass and accessibility problems. Answer with a verdict and justify. Save verdict + rationale to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md answers NO violations. Glass is applied to a floating control bar — a control/navigation surface, which is exactly where references/liquid-glass.md says Liquid Glass belongs. Must NOT fire 'icon-only buttons without accessibility labels': the controls use Label("Follow my location", …) with .labelStyle(.iconOnly), so the label text still supplies the accessibility name while only the icon renders. An agent that flags .labelStyle(.iconOnly) as an accessibility violation has pattern-matched on the modifier name without reasoning about what Label provides, and that is a failure. Hit targets are explicit (.frame(minWidth: 44, minHeight: 44) on each label) and the tracking control is a Toggle with .toggleStyle(.button), so selected state reaches VoiceOver via .isSelected rather than through a label that silently changes meaning — both were real defects in the pre-2026-08-04 fixture and neither should now be reported.

evals.name: onboarding-hero-clean
evals.prompt: Review fixtures/onboarding-hero.swift. Our reviewer says it contains a 'hero section', which we reject. Do you agree it should be restructured? Answer yes or no and justify. Save verdict + rationale to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md answers NO — do not restructure. The rejection reads 'hero section inside an app workflow'; first-run onboarding is not an app workflow, and a large lead visual is the platform norm there (Apple's own onboarding and what's-new sheets, and references/apple-native-design.md prefers 'illustration in empty/onboarding states'). Must engage the scope words 'inside app workflows' rather than matching the bare phrase 'hero section'. Credit for noting the screen is otherwise correct: semantic .largeTitle/.body fonts, the decorative SF Symbol carries .accessibilityHidden(true), its size is @ScaledMetric(relativeTo: .largeTitle) so it tracks Dynamic Type, and the content scrolls with the CTA pinned via .safeAreaInset so it cannot be stranded off-screen at AX3–AX5. Answering YES on keyword match is the failure.

evals.name: iphone-tab-root-clean
evals.prompt: Review fixtures/iphone-tab-root.swift, the root view of an iPhone app. Should this navigation structure change? Answer yes or no and justify. Save verdict + rationale to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md answers NO. Three flat co-equal top-level sections is exactly the topology TabView owns per references/navigation-patterns.md (flat top-level destinations → TabView), each wrapping its own NavigationStack for drill-down. The NavigationSplitView guidance is conditioned on collection/detail layouts 'when width supports it' — an iPhone root is neither. Proposing NavigationSplitView here is the failure. (This eval previously also guarded against treating TabView as suspect because eval 9 rejected it on iPad; that dirty case was cut 2026-08-21, but the same discipline applies: the topology decides the container, not the device class alone.)

evals.name: documented-custom-bar-clean
evals.prompt: Review fixtures/documented-custom-bar.swift. It replaces TabView with a hand-built bar. Should it be rewritten to use TabView? Answer yes or no and justify. Save verdict + rationale to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md answers NO. The rejection inventory in references/anti-web-smells.md states its hard-reject tier applies 'unless the user explicitly asks for it and the tradeoff is documented' — this fixture pays that toll in full: a dated approval, a load-bearing reason TabView cannot serve (SwiftUI exposes no control over system tab-bar height and no way to drive it from an in-progress DragGesture — a constraint no styling or accessory placement removes), an explicit record that TabView was prototyped and rejected on it, and delivered accessibility parity — a visible selected state via .symbolVariant that does not rely on color alone, .isSelected traits, 44pt minimum targets, and the score exposed as .accessibilityLabel plus .accessibilityValue so VoiceOver announces the number rather than replacing it. This eval tests whether the skill's own escape hatch is reachable in practice. Answering YES — rewriting to TabView despite the documented tradeoff — means the rejection list is being applied as absolute and the escape hatch is dead prose.

evals.name: fixed-frame-artwork-clean
evals.prompt: Review fixtures/poster-carousel.swift for Dynamic Type problems. Answer with a verdict and justify. Save verdict + rationale to ./verdict.md.
evals.expected_output: verdict.md answers NO disqualifying Dynamic Type violation. The guarded rejection is 'fixed-height rows that break Dynamic Type' / flagging the artwork frame: here the fixed dimensions constrain the AsyncImage artwork box, and artwork is not text — images do not need to scale with type size (the Apple media pattern). The caption carries no lineLimit and no height cap, and uses .fixedSize(horizontal: false, vertical: true), so it wraps and grows vertically with the user's type size instead of truncating. Flagging the artwork frame as a Dynamic Type violation is the failure this eval catches. Observations about quality at accessibility sizes — the fixed 120pt caption column producing narrow text towers at AX sizes, or .caption being small for identifying text — are legitimate non-blocking findings and may be reported at 'noticeable weakness'/'polish' severity without failing this eval; calling them disqualifying or 'must fix before ship' is over-flagging. Note the pre-2026-08-04 fixture did truncate (lineLimit(2) inside a width-constrained column) and the cold baseline correctly caught it — that defect is fixed, so re-reporting truncation now is wrong.
